section_summary: This section contains records concerning the 'second-generation Japanese problem' (Nisei), comprising prospectuses, news clippings, and an extensive consular report prepared in September 1935 by U.S. Consul Richard F. Boyce in Yokohama. The materials document the educational institutions, boarding facilities, and cultural organizations established in Japan to accommodate American-born Japanese youths, including the School for Foreign-Born Japanese, Waseda International Institute, and the Kaigai Kyoiku Kyokai. Consul Boyce's report provides an in-depth analysis of the social, linguistic, and economic challenges confronting these American citizens in Japan, as well as questions of dual nationality and cultural allegiance.

subfiles.about: An informational catalogue describing the courses of instruction, guidance services, and tuition fees of the School for Foreign-Born Japanese in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Prospectus of the School for Foreign-Born Japanese, linked to the Tokyo YMCA: two-year and special language courses, culture lectures, guidance, dormitory and employment help under Kazuya Matsumiya, with fees.
subfiles.title: Catalogue of the School for Foreign-Born Japanese

subfiles.about: A bilingual English and Japanese prospectus outlining the founding, curriculum, regulations, and officers of the Waseda International Institute.
subfiles.summary: Issued in April 1935 by Waseda Hoshien and Waseda University, this booklet announces the establishment of the Waseda International Institute to prepare overseas and American-born Japanese high school graduates for university entrance. It discusses the economic conditions and depression factors driving Nisei to seek educational and business opportunities in Japan, detailing courses in Japanese, Chinese, English, mathematics, and culture. The publication sets forth school terms, entrance requirements, living expenses, and dormitory facilities at Scott Hall, and presents the leadership roster, including President Tadaoki Yamamoto and Dr. H. B. Benninghoff, along with historical sketches of Waseda University and Waseda Hoshien.
subfiles.title: Prospectus of Waseda International Institute (Enclosure No. 2(d))

subfiles.about: An illustrated Japanese prospectus and admission guide detailing the preparatory school and dormitories of the Kaigai Kyoiku Kyokai at Inada-Noborito.
subfiles.summary: Published in June 1935 by the Kaigai Kyoiku Kyokai (Institute for the Education of Overseas Japanese), this guide describes its newly established Western-style dormitories and supplementary school at Masugatayama in Inada-Noborito. It details the association's mission to educate second-generation Japanese youths from overseas so they can serve as international bridges of peace and cooperation between Japan and their resident countries. The pamphlet lists distinguished officers, including President Viscount Kikujiro Ishii and several Cabinet ministers, while explaining admission qualifications, fees, courses of study, and application procedures.
subfiles.title: Dormitory and School Admission Guide of Kaigai Kyoiku Kyokai (Enclosure No. 2(c))

subfiles.about: An English translation of the prospectus and regulations of the Kaigai Kyoiku Kyokai (Institute for the Education of Overseas Japanese).
subfiles.summary: Translation of a Kaigai Kyoiku Kyokai circular: dormitory for ninety boarders near Tokyo, 23-hour weekly curriculum, admission for overseas Nisei aged twelve and older, and board members including Ishii, Okada, Hirota and Matsuda.
subfiles.title: English Translation of Kaigai Kyoiku Kyokai Pamphlet (Enclosure No. 2(c))

subfiles.about: A feature article exploring the identity, societal challenges, and economic barriers confronting American-born Japanese youth in both the United States and Japan.
subfiles.from: T. H. Shimanouchi, The Japan Advertiser
subfiles.summary: T. H. Shimanouchi's February 17, 1935 Japan Advertiser article: economic discrimination in the U.S. pushes college-educated Nisei toward Japan despite American loyalty; he urges Japanese to see them as American citizens and white Americans to end racial barriers.
subfiles.title: 'Second Generation Cast in Hard Role' by T. H. Shimanouchi (Enclosure No. 3(a))

subfiles.about: A newspaper feature reporting on the careers and cultural experiences of four American-born Japanese female stage performers working in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Japan Times & Mail profile of four American-born women performers in Tokyo, Fumiko Kawabata, Helen Honda, Betty Inada and Helen Sumida, popularizing jazz, tap and hula dancing and describing cultural misunderstandings.
subfiles.title: 'Second Generation Girls Introducing American Dance' (Enclosure No. 3(b))

subfiles.about: A voluntary consular report detailing the classifications, educational facilities, social difficulties, and political implications of second-generation Japanese living in Japan.
subfiles.from: Consul Richard F. Boyce, American Consulate, Yokohama
subfiles.summary: In this voluntary consular report dated September 20, 1935, Consul Richard F. Boyce analyzes the influx of American citizens of Japanese race into Japan during the Great Depression. Boyce divides the second generation into three distinct classes, focusing on 'Group C'—young adults educated in the United States or Hawaii who relocated to Tokyo for study or employment. The report details the severe linguistic, dietary, housing, and social challenges they face, reviews specialized schools and dormitories catering to them (including Waseda International Institute, Kaigai Kyoiku Kyokai, Nichibei Home, and Keisen Jogakuen), and examines their student clubs, official Japanese cultural propaganda efforts, and U.S. Foreign Service policy.
subfiles.title: The Second-Generation Japanese Problem
